additions.reason: Wisdom is the central concept of this Torah. The Rebbe teaches 'כִּי הַחָכְמָה הוּא בַּפָּנִים' — wisdom IS the face. Wisdom is not the cause of the face shining; wisdom and the face share the same essential nature. The verse from Kohelet (8:1) 'חָכְמַת אָדָם תָּאִיר פָּנָיו' grounds this bechina: wisdom illuminates/IS the face.

The face is the bechina of wisdom. The teaching states explicitly 'חָכְמַת אָדָם תָּאִיר פָּנָיו' — a man's wisdom illuminates his face — and then draws the equation: when the student receives his teacher's wisdom, he receives his face. The face is not merely lit by wisdom; it IS the outward form of wisdom.
additions.source_quote: כְּשֶׁהַתַּלְמִיד מְקַבֵּל חָכְמַת רַבּוֹ הוּא מְקַבֵּל פָּנָיו

additions.reason: The teacher's wisdom is the specific instantiation of חכמה in this Torah. Receiving the teacher's wisdom and receiving the teacher's face are described as the same act — making חָכְמַת הָרַב and פְּנֵי הָרַב bechinas of each other, and both bechinas of the general חכמה-פנים equivalence.
additions.source_quote: כְּשֶׁהַתַּלְמִיד מְקַבֵּל חָכְמַת רַבּוֹ הוּא מְקַבֵּל פָּנָיו

additions.reason: The teacher's face is a bechina of the teacher's wisdom. The Torah equates them: receiving wisdom = receiving the face. Furthermore, the student who gazes at his teacher's face while receiving the wisdom internalizes that face — which is why the student's face later carries the imprint of the teacher's wisdom. The face of the teacher is the concrete form of the abstract wisdom.
additions.source_quote: וּבִשְׁבִיל זֶה צָרִיךְ לְהִסְתַּכֵּל בִּפְנֵי רַבּוֹ בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁמְּקַבֵּל חָכְמָתוֹ

analysis_notes.torah_summary: Torah #230 is a very short teaching (two sentences) that establishes one core bechina: wisdom (חכמה) IS the face (פנים), grounded in Kohelet 8:1. The practical consequence (eitza) is that a student who receives his teacher's wisdom receives his teacher's face — so a perceptive person can look at a student's face and identify who his teacher is. The Torah cites Isaiah 30:20 ('your eyes shall see your teacher') as support for the practice of gazing at one's teacher while receiving wisdom.
